headline: High: shared MCP and overlapping file/network surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks; TREK’s sensitive travel data raises compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Semantic Kernel can use MCP servers and plugin function calling, while TREK also exposes MCP and runs a real-time collaborative AI workflow. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if TREK content is fed into Semantic Kernel or vice versa. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF TREK content is passed into Semantic Kernel prompts or plugins without provenance tagging, injection risk materializes.
IF either agent treats MCP tool output as trusted instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Add provenance labels to all MCP/tool outputs.
Strip or sandbox untrusted text before prompt assembly.
Disable automatic execution of tool suggestions.
Review one end-to-end message path for instruction leakage.
requires-engineering: enforce allowlisted tool schemas.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Semantic Kernel handles model provider API keys and plugin credentials, and TREK touches API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and user accounts. Both have filesystem surfaces and network egress, so a shared workspace or copied context could leak sensitive travel data or secrets to inference backends. No isolation mechanism is documented for the pair.
conditions: IF the two agents share files or logs, sensitive TREK data can enter Semantic Kernel context.
IF either agent forwards file contents to a third-party model API, secrets may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and log directories.
Redact secrets before any model call.
Disable file ingestion for sensitive folders.
Rotate exposed API keys after testing.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Semantic Kernel can write the filesystem and call MCP/OpenAPI tools; TREK writes ./data/travel.db and ./uploads/ and is collaborative in real time. Overlapping write authority on shared mutable resources can cause lost updates or corrupted state, even though neither profile shows git writes. The conflict is plausible in default collaborative setups.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or database, concurrent writes can collide.
IF MCP tools expose the same mutable resource to both agents, last-write-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign distinct storage paths per agent.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Enable database transactions and locking.
Audit shared MCP tools for mutable operations.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency controls.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Semantic Kernel is a general orchestration layer that can emit tool calls and structured outputs, while TREK is a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in. If TREK consumes Semantic Kernel output as authoritative, a mistaken itinerary, budget, or reservation action can cascade into user-visible errors. The pairwise interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty stays at medium.
conditions: IF TREK uses Semantic Kernel output without verification, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF either agent auto-executes downstream actions from the other’s text, errors become user-visible.
mitigations: Insert human review before bookings or edits.
Require schema validation on exchanged outputs.
Cross-check itinerary facts against source APIs.
Log and diff all agent-to-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating for actions.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly touches travel plans, reservations, country visit history, email addresses, and MFA secrets, which can include regulated personal data. Semantic Kernel is a library with broad network egress and plugin credentials handling, but no residency or retention controls are documented. The mismatch is compliance-relevant because TREK’s sensitive data could flow into a less constrained processing path.
conditions: IF TREK data includes EU PII or sensitive travel history, processing through unconstrained model APIs may breach policy.
IF logs retain reservations or MFA secrets, retention and subject-rights obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Classify TREK fields by sensitivity.
Block secrets from prompts and logs.
Confirm residency and DPA coverage for model endpoints.
Set short log retention on sensitive tables.
requires-engineering: implement deletion/export workflows.
